cases.presenting_complaint: Worsening depression despite long-term anxiety medication use
cases.duration: Depression worsening: 8 months. Benzodiazepine use: 4 years
cases.associated: Using alprazolam 2-3mg daily (more than prescribed), running out early each month, borrowing from friends, mood worsening despite medication, sedation affecting daily function, memory problems, relationship strain from medication-seeking behavior, anxiety returns within hours of dose, depression with anhedonia and hopelessness
cases.risk_factors: Long-term benzodiazepine prescription for anxiety (started 4 years ago), gradual dose escalation, no previous substance use disorder but developing dependence, doctor shopping (multiple prescriptions), recent stressors (divorce), personality traits (impulsive)
cases.mse: Appearance: Sedated, slow movements. Behavior: Anxious about running out of medication. Speech: Slurred, slow. Mood: 'I need my medicine to function'. Affect: Depressed, anxious. Thought: Preoccupation with medication, no psychosis. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Impaired short-term memory. Insight: Partial - knows she uses more than prescribed but feels she needs it
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal. PHQ-9: 18/27. Urine toxicology: Alprazolam positive, no other substances. Prescriptions reviewed: multiple benzodiazepine prescriptions from different doctors. GGT elevated (alcohol use suggested but denied)
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Depressed mood, benzodiazepine dependence, social stressors. Benzodiazepines can worsen depression and increase impulsivity
cases.explanation: This patient has developed benzodiazepine dependence (prescription drug misuse) complicating underlying anxiety and depression. Long-term benzodiazepine use (>2-4 weeks) leads to tolerance, dependence, and worsening of original anxiety (rebound anxiety between doses). Paradoxically, benzodiazepines can worsen depression and cause cognitive impairment. The patient is showing features of sedative/hypnotic use disorder: escalating dose, doctor shopping, unsuccessful attempts to cut down, preoccupation with use. Treatment requires careful benzodiazepine taper while managing underlying anxiety/depression with appropriate alternatives
cases.management: (1) URGENT: Address benzodiazepine misuse - explain risks to patient; (2) Arrange supervised benzodiazepine taper (reduce 10-25% every 1-2 weeks); (3) Convert to long-acting benzodiazepine (diazepam) for easier taper; (4) Taper may take months; (5) SSRI for underlying anxiety/depression (takes 4-6 weeks to work, so start early); (6) Avoid benzodiazepines in future; (7) Add non-pharmacological anxiety treatment: CBT, relaxation; (8) Address doctor shopping - coordinate care with all prescribers; (9) Support for dependence: counseling, possibly support groups; (10) Address divorce stress; (11) Monitor for withdrawal symptoms and depression during taper; (12) Treat underlying anxiety with appropriate long-term agents; (13) Regular follow-up; (14) Avoid opioids or other sedatives

cases.diagnosis: Depression in Patient with History of Stroke
cases.presenting_complaint: Persistent low mood and tearfulness since stroke 6 months ago
cases.associated: Left-sided weakness affecting dominant hand, difficulty speaking (mild aphasia), frustration with communication, withdrawal from rehabilitation, sadness about loss of function, dependence on wife for ADLs, sleep disturbance, reduced appetite, hopelessness about recovery, passive death wishes
cases.risk_factors: Right MCA stroke 6 months ago, hypertension, diabetes, left hemiparesis affecting dominant hand, pre-stroke mild depression (untreated), social isolation (stroke reduced mobility), wife also elderly with health issues, limited rehabilitation attendance
cases.mse: Appearance: Left arm in sling, appears frail. Behavior: Frustrated when trying to speak. Speech: Mild dysarthria, word-finding difficulty. Mood: 'I'm useless now'. Affect: Depressed, tearful. Thought: Hopeless about recovery, worthlessness. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Mild executive dysfunction, otherwise intact. Insight: Partial - understands stroke impact but demoralized
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal, Hb normal. PHQ-9: 16/27. CT brain: Right MCA infarct, no new changes. Speech therapy assessment: mild expressive aphasia. NIHSS: 4 (mild-moderate)
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Elderly with disability, hopelessness, passive SI, limited social support. Stroke patients have elevated suicide risk
cases.explanation: Post-stroke depression affects 30-40% of patients, with highest risk in first year. This patient has clear temporal relationship between stroke and depressive symptoms. Risk factors: left frontal lesion (common in depression), physical disability, loss of independence, communication difficulties, and pre-existing depression. Depression worsens rehabilitation outcomes - motivated patients recover better. Aphasia complicates assessment and treatment. Passive death wishes require monitoring but may reflect realistic adjustment. Prognosis depends on physical recovery and psychological support
cases.management: (1) Treat depression: SSRI (e.g., sertraline 50-100mg) - also may aid recovery (neuroplasticity); (2) Intensive rehabilitation - PT, OT, speech therapy; (3) Encourage rehabilitation attendance despite low mood; (4) Address hopelessness - set realistic small goals; (5) Communication strategies given aphasia; (6) Involve wife in care and therapy; (7) Family psychoeducation; (8) Social engagement within limitations; (9) Community stroke support groups; (10) Address pre-stroke depression; (11) Monitor for cognitive changes; (12) Cardiovascular risk factor management; (13) Consider if aphasia affects reporting - use observational assessment; (14) Long-term follow-up

cases.presenting_complaint: Worsening depression and headaches for 1 year
cases.associated: Migraines 15-20 days/month (chronic migraine), unilateral throbbing headaches with photophobia and nausea, medication overuse (taking triptans 10+ days/month), depression, hopelessness about chronic pain, reduced work days, social isolation, sleep disturbance (migraines disrupt sleep), fatigue, anhedonia, passive SI during severe migraine attacks
cases.risk_factors: Chronic migraine with medication overuse, frequent headaches limiting function, job loss due to migraines, social isolation, family history of migraines (mother), previous depression, current financial stress, limited access to specialist care
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriately dressed but appears tired. Behavior: Discusses headaches cautiously (worries about being seen as complaining). Speech: Normal. Mood: 'I'm tired of living with pain'. Affect: Depressed, frustrated. Thought: Hopeless about pain, no active SI but 'can't imagine living like this forever'. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Good - knows depression and pain interact
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal. PHQ-9: 17/27. Headache diary: 18 headache days/month. Medication overuse confirmed (triptans >10 days/month). MRI brain: Normal. Neurology review: Chronic migraine, medication overuse headache
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Chronic pain with disability, hopelessness, passive SI during migraines. Chronic pain patients have elevated suicide risk
cases.explanation: This patient has comorbid Major Depressive Disorder, Chronic Migraine (15+ headache days/month for >3 months), and Medication Overuse Headache (MOH). Bidirectional relationship: depression worsens pain perception and treatment adherence, migraines cause disability leading to low mood. MOH develops from frequent triptan use - requires withdrawal. Treating depression is essential but headache management must also be addressed. Chronic migraine has significant disability impact (work, social). Pain catastrophizing may be present. Cultural factor: tendency to minimize pain complaints, under-treat
cases.management: (1) Treat depression: SSRI or SNRI (e.g., venlafaxine - also helps migraines); (2) Address medication overuse: structured withdrawal program; (3) Preventive migraine treatment: CGRP monoclonal antibodies if available, topiramate, propranolol; (4) Acute treatment optimization (not triptans for MOH); (5) Headache diary for tracking; (6) CBT for chronic pain and depression; (7) Address pain catastrophizing; (8) Sleep hygiene (both affect each other); (9) Trigger identification and management; (10) Job counseling - accommodate migraines; (11) Address financial stress; (12) Social support; (13) Coordinate with neurologist; (14) Expect improvement over months with comprehensive treatment; (15) Long-term management

cases.diagnosis: Depression with Comorbid Generalized Anxiety Disorder
cases.presenting_complaint: Chronic worry and low mood that have worsened over the past year
cases.associated: Excessive worry about health (own and family), children, finances, and future; difficulty controlling worry; muscle tension; restlessness; fatigue; sleep disturbance; poor concentration; multiple doctor visits for health worries; recent low mood, anhedonia, and hopelessness; symptoms interfere with daily functioning
cases.risk_factors: Generalized Anxiety Disorder for 15 years (suboptimally treated), history of childhood anxiety, recent menopausal transition (3 years ago), financial stressors, elderly parents requiring care, son living abroad (worry about him), limited coping skills, family history of anxiety (sister)
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriately dressed, appears tense. Behavior: Restless, fidgeting. Speech: Normal rate but talks rapidly about worries. Mood: 'Everything feels overwhelming'. Affect: Anxious, depressed. Thought: Excessive worry about multiple domains, catastrophic thinking, feels 'something bad will happen'. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Poor concentration, reports memory issues. Insight: Good - knows she worries excessively
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal, estrogen low (postmenopausal). PHQ-9: 14/27. GAD-7: 18/21 (severe). ECG: Normal. Medical workup for health worries unremarkable
cases.suicide_risk: Low-moderate risk. No active SI but chronic distress, functional impairment. Anxiety may paradoxically be protective (fear of death) or risk (worst-case thinking)
cases.explanation: This patient has long-standing Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) with recent development/worsening of Major Depression. GAD and depression have high comorbidity (60%), often called 'mixed anxiety-depressive disorder' when both present. GAD typically precedes depression - chronic anxiety depletes resources, leads to avoidance and isolation, precipitating depression. Menopause may have contributed (estrogen decline affects mood). Health anxiety component significant. Poor treatment adherence likely contributed to chronicity. Prognosis better when both conditions treated together
cases.management: (1) SSRI or SNRI first-line for both conditions (e.g., venlafaxine XR 75-225mg, escitalopram 10-20mg); (2) CBT for GAD: cognitive restructuring of worry, worry exposure, relaxation training; (3) CBT for depression; (4) Mindfulness-based stress reduction; (5) Address health anxiety - reassurance scheduling, not doctor shopping; (6) Worry time scheduling; (7) Progressive muscle relaxation; (8) Sleep hygiene; (9) Exercise program; (10) Address financial/caregiving stressors; (11) Hormone replacement therapy discussion with gynecologist; (12) Family psychoeducation; (13) Long-term maintenance treatment; (14) Regular follow-up

cases.presenting_complaint: Recurrent panic attacks and low mood for 6 months
cases.associated: Panic attacks 4-5 times/week with palpitations, shortness of breath, dizziness, fear of dying, fear of places where escape difficult (agoraphobia), situational avoidance, ongoing low mood, anhedonia, sleep disturbance, reduced work attendance, worry about having attacks, isolation from fear of attack in public
cases.risk_factors: First-degree relative with panic disorder (cousin), perfectionism, recent work stress (new job 8 months ago), history of childhood anxiety, limited social support in new city, smoking (10 cigarettes/day, may increase anxiety)
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriately dressed, appears anxious. Behavior: Restless, hypervigilant. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'I'm afraid I'll have a heart attack and die'. Affect: Anxious, depressed. Thought: Fear of dying, catastrophe about panic attacks. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Concentration impaired. Insight: Partial - knows attacks aren't dangerous but can't stop fear
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal, ECG normal. PHQ-9: 15/27. GAD-7: 12/21. Panic Disorder Severity Scale: Moderate. Cardiology review: Normal cardiac workup. No substance use (beyond smoking)
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Anxiety can be protective (fear of death) but also distressing, isolation increases risk. No active SI
cases.explanation: This patient has comorbid Major Depressive Disorder and Panic Disorder with mild agoraphobia. Comorbidity is common (50-60% of panic disorder patients have depression). Bidirectional relationship: panic attacks cause disability and avoidance leading to low mood, depression worsens anxiety sensitivity. The patient shows good insight but catastrophic misinterpretation of physical symptoms persists. Agoraphobia is developing (avoidance of situations where escape might be difficult). Family history supports genetic predisposition. Treatment must address both panic (exposure) and depression (activation, cognitions)
cases.management: (1) SSRI first-line (e.g., sertraline 50-100mg, start low); (2) CBT for Panic Disorder: interoceptive exposure (deliberately induce symptoms to learn safety), cognitive restructuring, exposure to agoraphobic situations; (3) CBT for depression; (4) Breathing retraining; (5) Progressive desensitization to feared situations; (6) Address work stress; (7) Smoking cessation program; (8) Build local support network; (9) Avoid reassurance-seeking (doctor shopping); (10) Consider beta-blocker for performance anxiety if specific situations; (11) Mindfulness; (12) Long-term treatment; (13) Expect 8-12 weeks for full response; (14) Maintenance treatment

cases.presenting_complaint: Monthly mood swings and low mood worse before periods for 2 years
cases.associated: Low mood, irritability, and tearfulness in luteal phase (7-10 days before period), improved within days of period starting, bloating, breast tenderness, headaches, fatigue, food cravings, social withdrawal, relationship strain during luteal phase, work difficulties, anhedonia during symptomatic phase, suicidal ideation briefly during worst episodes
cases.risk_factors: PMDD (luteal phase only), history of postpartum depression, family history of mood disorders (mother had PMDD), stress, lack of exercise, irregular sleep, current oral contraceptive use (may worsen symptoms)
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate. Behavior: Normal during interview (follicular phase). Speech: Normal. Mood: 'Fine now but know it will come'. Affect: Mildly anxious. Thought: No psychosis. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Excellent - recognizes monthly pattern
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, prolactin normal, estradiol/progesterone normal for cycle phase. PHQ-9: 12/27 (during follicular phase). Prospectively tracked symptoms confirm PMDD diagnosis (symptoms present 7 days before period for 2+ cycles). Hormone levels appropriate
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk during severe luteal phase episodes. Passive SI during worst symptoms, but good insight and treatment seeking. Need safety plan for symptomatic phase
cases.explanation: Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD) is a severe form of premenstrual syndrome affecting 3-8% of women. Diagnosis requires prospective symptom tracking for 2 cycles showing symptoms in luteal phase only, resolving with menses. This patient meets criteria. Unlike PMS, PMDD causes significant impairment and distress. Depression during symptomatic phase is real but cyclical. Comorbid depression risk elevated. Treatment differs from chronic depression - focuses on luteal phase management. Oral contraceptives may worsen symptoms (some progestins)
cases.management: (1) Confirm PMDD with prospective tracking (done); (2) FIRST-LINE: SSRI (can be continuous or luteal phase only dosing) - e.g., sertraline 50-100mg; (3) Consider continuous vs. intermittent dosing; (4) If SSRI insufficient: consider oral contraceptive with drospirenone (Yaz approved for PMDD); (5) Calcium carbonate and vitamin B6 supplementation; (6) Regular exercise; (7) Sleep hygiene; (8) Stress management; (9) Cognitive behavioral strategies for luteal phase; (10) Dietary modifications (reduce caffeine, sugar, salt); (11) Safety plan for severe luteal phase; (12) Discuss future fertility plans (PMDD may improve with pregnancy, worsen postpartum); (13) Long-term management; (14) Monitor for breakthrough symptoms

cases.diagnosis: Depression with Internet Gaming Disorder in Adolescent
cases.presenting_complaint: School refusal, low mood, and excessive gaming discovered by parents
cases.associated: Gaming 6-8 hours daily (mostly after school), dropped out of school 2 months ago, sleep disruption (gaming until 3am), social withdrawal from friends, stopped sports, conflict with parents over gaming, lying about gaming time, poor academic performance, reduced appetite, anhedonia except during gaming, expressed hopelessness about future
cases.risk_factors: Internet Gaming Disorder (DSM-5 condition for further study), social anxiety (underlying), bullying at school (stopped attending due to teasing), family conflict, lack of real-world friends, introverted personality, easy access to gaming, pandemic increased isolation
cases.mse: Appearance: Casual, appears tired. Behavior: Reluctant to engage, defensive about gaming. Speech: Minimal. Mood: 'Leave me alone'. Affect: Depressed, irritable. Thought: Negative about school and future, no psychosis. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Intact but unmotivated. Insight: Poor - minimizes problem
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal. PHQ-9: 14/27. Gaming disorder assessment positive. School records: Attendance 40% before dropping out. Parents report significant conflict. No substance use
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. School refusal, isolation, hopelessness. Gaming as escape but may indicate underlying distress. Requires safety assessment
cases.explanation: This adolescent has comorbid Major Depressive Disorder and Internet Gaming Disorder. Gaming Disorder in adolescents is increasing - prevalence estimates vary (1-10%). Bidirectional relationship: underlying social anxiety/depression lead to escapist gaming, gaming causes school refusal and social isolation worsening depression. Bullying likely contributed to school refusal. Family conflict maintains the problem (confrontation increases gaming). Insight is poor (typical in adolescents). Treatment requires family involvement, addressing underlying depression/anxiety, and structured gaming reduction - not punishment but negotiation
cases.management: (1) Family assessment and intervention - reduce conflict; (2) Treat depression: SSRI (e.g., fluoxetine, approved for adolescents) if indicated; (3) Address gaming: gradual reduction with negotiated limits; (4) Return-to-school plan: may need temporary alternative (home tuition), address bullying; (5) CBT for depression and anxiety; (6) Social skills training; (7) Alternative activities (offline hobbies, sports if interest); (8) Parental monitoring (not surveillance) of gaming; (9) Sleep hygiene; (10) Family therapy for conflict; (11) Peer group for social connection; (12) Address underlying anxiety; (13) Educational planning; (14) Regular follow-up; (15) Consider residential if severe and family intervention fails

cases.diagnosis: Depression in Patient with Hepatitis C and Interferon Treatment
cases.presenting_complaint: Low mood, fatigue, and suicidal thoughts since starting hepatitis C treatment 3 months ago
cases.associated: Profound fatigue limiting daily activities, low mood, anhedonia, insomnia, poor appetite, cognitive complaints ('can't think straight'), irritability, passive and active suicidal ideation ('tired of feeling this way'), guilt about past behaviors (IV drug use), social isolation due to contagion fears
cases.risk_factors: Hepatitis C on interferon-alpha treatment (known to cause depression), previous history of depression (10 years ago), IV drug use history, social isolation, guilt about past, limited support (family estranged due to drug history), chronic illness burden
cases.mse: Appearance: Thin, appears ill. Behavior: Fatigued, slow. Speech: Normal rate. Mood: 'I can't cope with this treatment'. Affect: Depressed, hopeless. Thought: Active suicidal ideation (has thought about overdose), guilt about past, no psychosis. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Cognitive complaints, likely interferon-related. Insight: Partial - knows interferon causing symptoms but feels unable to continue
cases.investigations: Blood: HCV RNA positive, LFTs elevated, TSH normal, B12 normal. PHQ-9: 22/27 (severe). Hepatitis C viral load being treated. Depression emerged 8 weeks into interferon (typical). No substance use currently
cases.suicide_risk: HIGH RISK. Active suicidal ideation with interferon treatment (known risk), previous depression history, isolation, chronic illness. Interferon-associated depression can be severe
cases.explanation: Interferon-alpha treatment for Hepatitis C is well-known to cause depression in 20-40% of patients, with onset typically 4-12 weeks into treatment. This patient has interferon-induced depression, potentially triggered recurrence of previous depression. Depression can be severe with suicidal ideation - interferon crosses blood-brain barrier affecting serotonin and dopamine. Current guidelines recommend: antidepressant prophylaxis in high-risk patients, close monitoring, treatment discontinuation if severe. This patient needs urgent psychiatric assessment regarding treatment continuation and depression management
cases.management: URGENT: (1) Comprehensive suicide risk assessment; (2) Discuss with hepatologist about treatment continuation; (3) Start antidepressant immediately (SSRI - e.g., sertraline 50-100mg); (4) Monitor depression severity weekly; (5) Consider interferon dose reduction or discontinuation if severe; (6) NEWER AGENTS: discuss DAAs (direct-acting antivirals) with hepatologist - lower depression risk than interferon. TREATMENT: (7) SSRI for interferon-induced depression; (8) Support and counseling; (9) Address guilt about past; (10) Social support - reconnect with family if possible; (11) Psychoeducation about treatment-related depression; (12) Regular follow-up; (13) If no improvement: consider antidepressant change or addition; (14) Crisis plan; (15) Hepatitis C support groups

cases.presenting_complaint: Low mood and difficulty quitting smoking despite knowing it's harming her
cases.associated: Smoking 15 cigarettes daily, multiple quit attempts failed, mood worsens when trying to quit (irritability, low mood), using smoking to cope with stress and depression, heavy smoking in morning, concealment of smoking from family, chronic cough, financial strain from smoking, passive SI during worst depressive periods
cases.risk_factors: Nicotine dependence (20 years), unsuccessful quit attempts, comorbid depression, stress, social smoking in peer group, family history of addiction (father), childhood trauma, limited coping skills
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriate, smells of smoke. Behavior: Fidgety, defensive about smoking. Speech: Normal. Mood: 'I know smoking is killing me but I can't stop'. Affect: Depressed, ashamed. Thought: No psychosis. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Partial - knows smoking harmful but feels addicted
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal, cotinine positive. PHQ-9: 14/27. Fagerström Test: 6/10 (moderate dependence). Spirometry: Mild obstruction (early COPD). No current substance use beyond nicotine
cases.suicide_risk: Low-moderate risk. No active SI, but smoking and depression both increase long-term mortality risk. Shame about addiction
cases.explanation: This patient has comorbid Major Depressive Disorder and Nicotine Dependence. Bidirectional relationship: depression increases smoking prevalence (2x higher than general population), nicotine temporarily improves mood but worsens depression long-term, quitting often worsens mood temporarily (nicotine withdrawal). This creates cycle - smoking used to cope with depression, but smoking maintains depression. Many smokers with depression use smoking for self-medication (nicotine has antidepressant effects short-term). Treatment must address both - antidepressants can help both conditions (bupropion is particularly useful)
cases.management: (1) Treat depression: SSRI (e.g., sertraline 50-100mg) or bupropion (treats both depression and smoking); (2) Smoking cessation: combination pharmacotherapy (bupropion + NRT); (3) Varenicline effective but monitor mood; (4) Behavioral support for quitting; (5) Address underlying depression driving smoking; (6) CBT for both conditions; (7) Avoid quit attempts during acute depression (failure risk); (8) Expect temporary worsening of mood during quit attempt; (9) Set realistic goals; (10) Reduce rather than immediate quit initially; (11) Address triggers; (12) Social support; (13) Financial counseling; (14) Long-term follow-up; (15) COPD monitoring

cases.presenting_complaint: Loss of faith and existential despair following near-death experience 6 months ago
cases.associated: Loss of meaning and purpose, questioning religious beliefs, existential despair, anhedonia, sleep disturbance, guilt about loss of faith, family conflict (devout family upset by his questioning), isolation from religious community, passive death wishes ('if there's no afterlife, what's the point'), hopelessness, reduced functioning
cases.risk_factors: Near-death experience (cardiac arrest with 5-minute downtime) 6 months ago, previous strong religious faith (devout Catholic), survivor guilt (others died in same incident), limited processing of NDE, family conflict about beliefs, existential crisis, previous depression history (postpartum)
cases.mse: Appearance: Appropriately dressed but appears distressed. Behavior: Reflective, questioning. Speech: Normal but discusses existential topics. Mood: 'Everything I believed was a lie'. Affect: Depressed, anxious. Thought: Existential concerns, questioning meaning, no psychosis. Perception: No abnormality. Cognition: Intact. Insight: Partial - recognizes NDE changed him
cases.investigations: Blood: TSH normal, B12 normal. PHQ-9: 15/27. Spiritual/existential assessment needed. Cardiac workup post-arrest normal. No substance use
cases.suicide_risk: Moderate risk. Existential despair, passive SI related to loss of meaning. NDE survivors have elevated suicide risk
cases.explanation: This patient has Major Depression precipitated by a near-death experience and subsequent existential/spiritual crisis. NDEs can be profoundly life-altering, sometimes causing depression when they conflict with prior beliefs. The patient is experiencing 'existential depression' - loss of meaning and purpose. Family conflict compounds distress. Loss of religious community is isolating. This differs from typical depression - treatment must address spiritual/existential dimensions. NDE processing and meaning-making are important. Faith traditions vary in how they interpret NDEs - patient may need to find new framework
cases.management: (1) Treat depression: SSRI (e.g., sertraline 50-100mg); (2) Grief work for loss of previous worldview; (3) Existential psychotherapy; (4) NDE integration support - there are specific resources for NDE processing; (5) Explore meaning and purpose beyond previous framework; (6) Respect patient's journey - don't push return to previous faith; (7) Family therapy to address conflict; (8) Support finding new spiritual community or practice if desired; (9) Mindfulness and acceptance-based approaches; (10) Address survivor guilt; (11) Connect with other NDE survivors if available; (12) Philosophical/existential reading if patient interested; (13) Gradual return to function; (14) Long-term support; (15) Crisis intervention if SI escalates
